title: Summer Greetings from Japan

history.note: Title page typed line by line as printed.

summary: Walter L. Sheldon, the leader of the St. Louis Ethical Society, spent about two months in Japan in the summer of 1906, and these are the sixteen letters he wrote home to his wife, published by her after his death. He sails from Vancouver on the Empress of India in May, stays at the Hotel Metropole in Tokyo, and through Anna C. Hartshorne and Miss Tsuda of the girls’ school they ran meets university professors, teachers, and officials; he visits schools and temples, the slums of Tokyo and the iris gardens at Horikiri, goes to Kamakura, lectures to Japanese students, and moves on to Kyoto and Nikko in July. The letters are mostly about Japanese thought, religion, education, and manners as he saw them, with sixteen of his own snapshots. An introductory letter by Anna C. Hartshorne opens the book.

notes_on_text: The book has no printed contents; the place and date after each letter in the contents are the editor’s, taken from the letter’s heading (the fifteenth letter is dated only “Sunday A. M.”: Sunday was 15 July).
Each photograph is printed on a leaf of its own, bound just before the letter it was enclosed in; here it follows that letter’s heading.

The introductory letter is by Anna C. Hartshorne, who died in 1957; the book is in the public domain in the United States and Japan, and may still be in copyright in countries where the term is the author’s life and 70 years.
